title: Ballot Buddy · California

boxes.title: How to read this
boxes.html: This report does not tell you who to vote for. It lays out who wrote the checks and what the public record shows. A donation is a fact about the donor; it is not proof of what the candidate will do.

footer: Sources. Who ran and who won: the Nov 3, 2026 results in the Results tab. Federal money: FEC bulk files, downloaded Nov 2, 2026. Records and positions: linked per item. California state-race money isn't in the guide yet, so those candidates have no money meters.

races.title: Governor
races.note: The top two finishers from the Nov 3, 2026 count. Everyone else in this race is coming.

cands.name: Xavier Becerra
cands.bio: Democrat and Stanford-trained attorney from Sacramento. Former deputy attorney general, one-term state Assemblymember (1990–92), U.S. Representative (1993–2017), California Attorney General (2017–2021) and U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (2021–2025). Governor-elect of California.

controversies.text: In January 2019, Attorney General Becerra's office told two UC Berkeley reporters that possessing a list of convicted police officers was a misdemeanor, and demanded they destroy it. The First Amendment Coalition called a threat of charges groundless. His office said the data was confidential. The reporters refused to comply.

In May 2026, KQED reported that Becerra's time as U.S. health secretary had drawn new scrutiny from journalists and opponents, including over the migrant child crisis. His own response is not covered here.

endorsements.text: Endorsed by U.S. Reps. Salud Carbajal, Gil Cisneros, James Clyburn, Jasmine Crockett, Tony Cárdenas, Ted Lieu, Raul Ruiz and Mark Takano, per Ballotpedia.
Endorsed by SEIU Local 521, Equality California and California Young Democrats, per Ballotpedia.

cands.gaps: We found no stated positions or actions from Becerra on data centers; his campaign site has an AI page, but only a short summary was readable. We found nothing on eliminating homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign buyers of homes and land, gun laws, school choice or teacher pay, or H-1B and immigration enforcement. His record on policing is mixed in the sources we read, and we could not cover it fully. The Ballotpedia page was cut off partway through the Senate roll call. We did not read court or primary agency records for the controversies listed, only a Wikipedia summary. He did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey, so we have no questionnaire answers.

qual.why: He has prior statewide executive office and led a very large federal department, plus long legislative leadership. Those fit the high tier for a state chief executive. Reporting also records criticism of his management in some roles.

back-police-order.evidence: As Attorney General he directed operations against MS-13 and Norteño street gangs and the Country Boy Crips in 2018–2019.

cands.name: Steve Hilton
cands.bio: British-born American political commentator and Republican candidate for California governor in 2026. Director of strategy for UK Prime Minister David Cameron 2010–2012, co-founder and CEO of the tech start-up Crowdpac until 2018, and Fox News host (2017–2023) and contributor. He holds no elected office.

endorsements.text: Donald Trump endorsed Hilton on April 6, 2026.
U.S. Reps. Kevin Kiley and Tom McClintock are listed among his endorsers.
Vivek Ramaswamy endorsed Hilton.

cands.gaps: We found no documented stance or action from Hilton on data centers, restrictions on institutional or foreign buyers of homes and land, gun laws, abortion, or the H-1B program. He has not held office, so there is no legislative or executive record to review. The page we read does not detail his work at Crowdpac, such as its size or budget, or the scope of his role under David Cameron. Hilton did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey, so his platform comes only from his campaign website as quoted by Ballotpedia.

cands.name: Gloria Romero
cands.bio: Former California Senate Majority Leader (2005–2008), the first woman in that role. Represented Senate District 24 from 2001 to 2010 after election to the Assembly in 1998. Professor emeritus and education reform advocate. Author of the 'parent trigger' law. Left the Democratic Party for the Republican Party in 2024.

endorsements.text: Republican Party of California
Reform California

cands.gaps: We could not find where Gloria Romero was born or when she moved to California, if she did. We found nothing documenting her stance on data centers, development or growth limits, homestead property taxes, foreign or institutional land buying, abortion, or gun laws. We also found nothing on her record on immigration enforcement or H-1B. We found no documented controversies. The pages we had do not show how she voted on specific bills in the Legislature. Her stated priorities on fire mitigation and homebuilding regulation were too general to match to a specific position.

cands.name: Fiona Ma
cands.bio: Certified public accountant and California's 34th State Treasurer since January 2019. Earlier served on the State Board of Equalization (2014–2019), in the State Assembly (2006–2012, Speaker pro Tempore 2010–2012) and on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors (2002–2006). Lieutenant Governor-elect.

controversies.text: A former staffer, Judith Blackwell, sued in 2021 alleging Ma exposed herself and climbed into her bed when they shared rooms on work stays. A judge let the harassment claims go to trial. In 2024 the state agreed to pay $350,000. Ma denied it, called the suit frivolous, and called the settlement vindication.

endorsements.text: California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO (listed as sole labor federation endorsement), California Nurses Association, Equality California, IUOE Local 3 and National Union of Healthcare Workers endorsed her 2026 Lieutenant Governor campaign.
Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis, Secretary of State Shirley Weber, the Teamsters, LIUNA and California Professional Firefighters are listed as endorsers on her campaign site.

cands.gaps: We could not find when Fiona Ma moved to California or any details of her childhood beyond her New York schooling. We found no documented statements from her on data centers or on new development. We found no specific actions or statements by her tied to homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign land buyers, H-1B or immigration enforcement, police pay, gun laws, abortion or school choice. Her campaign survey says she supports immigrant communities and coastal protection, but those statements are general. The pages did not show how she handled the Board of Equalization audits' outcomes beyond her own and Wikipedia's accounts.

local.label: Roots 55: She was born and schooled in New York, and the record shows her in San Francisco public roles from 1995 (Assessment Appeals Board appointment, district representative for a state senator) and in elected California office since 2002, but her arrival date is not stated.

score.why: Raised $0, under $50,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.

qual.background: Statewide elected California Treasurer since 2019, overseeing roughly $3 trillion in annual payments, a $124 billion investment portfolio and $93 billion in outstanding bonds. Chaired the Board of Equalization (ordered three external audits), served as Assembly Majority Whip and Speaker pro Tempore, served on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, and has been a CPA since 1992 with her own accounting firm.
qual.why: Prior statewide executive office, a large public budget and bond portfolio, years of legislative leadership and agency chair experience fit the high tier for a chief-executive role.
qual.label: Prior statewide executive office, a large public budget and bond portfolio, years of legislative leadership and agency chair experience fit the high tier for a chief-executive role.

races.note: The top two finishers from the Nov 3, 2026 count. Everyone else in this race is coming.

cands.name: Michael E. Gates
cands.bio: Michael E. Gates is a Republican attorney and the Huntington Beach resident who ran for California Attorney General in 2026. He was a litigator and trial attorney, then a partner at an Orange County law firm. He served as Huntington Beach City Attorney for ten years after his 2014 election. Ballotpedia also lists work as a U.S. Department of Justice lawyer.

endorsements.text: Republican Party of California, Orange County Republican Party and many other county Republican parties, per Ballotpedia's endorsement list.
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and California Rifle & Pistol Association, per Ballotpedia's list.
Police groups including the Redlands Police Officers Association, Newport Beach Police Association and, per his own survey, the Huntington Beach Police Officers' Association.

Individuals he lists in his survey include Steve Hilton, Carl DeMaio, Tony Strickland, Gloria Romero, Tony Rackauckas, Steve Garvey and Don Barnes. Ballotpedia separately lists State Assm. Jeff Gonzalez.

cands.gaps: We could not find Gates's birthplace, where he was raised, or when he came to California; 'lifelong Californian' is his own description. We found no details of his Huntington Beach City Attorney record, such as cases, opinions or policies, and no details of his U.S. Department of Justice role or his state bar standing. We found no documented actions or statements on data centers, homestead property taxes, foreign or investor land buying, growth and land use, H-1B or immigration enforcement, guns, abortion or school choice. No controversies turned up in the pages reviewed.

score.why: Raised $0, under $50,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.
score.why_money: Raised $0, under $50,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.

qual.background: Litigator and trial attorney who became a partner at an Orange County firm, elected Huntington Beach City Attorney in 2014, 2018 and 2022 (ten years), and listed by Ballotpedia as having worked as a lawyer with the U.S. Department of Justice.
qual.why: Long litigation practice and ten years as an elected city attorney are strong, relevant legal experience. The score stops short of the top because the pages don't show his state bar standing, the details of his DOJ work, or any statewide or criminal appellate work.

cands.name: Rob Bonta
cands.bio: Attorney General of California since April 2021. Yale Law graduate, former Keker & Van Nest litigation associate and San Francisco Deputy City Attorney (2003–2012). Served on the Alameda City Council (2010–2012) and in the State Assembly for District 18 (2012–2021). First Filipino American in the Legislature and as AG.

controversies.text: In June 2022, a state Justice Department firearms dashboard briefly exposed personal data of people who applied for concealed-carry permits between 2011 and 2021, including names, addresses and, in some cases, driver's license numbers. The data was online under 24 hours. Bonta called it "unacceptable" and said he was "deeply disturbed and angered." Lawsuits followed.

CalMatters reported that, while in the Assembly, Bonta paid $25,000 from his foundation to the nonprofit where his wife worked. It also reported he helped her employers raise over $560,000, largely from companies that lobby the Legislature. The practice is legal, though ethics experts called it inappropriate. His spokesman said the foundation now bars funds going to any group employing either Bonta.

endorsements.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris (2026 campaign)
Democratic Party of California (2026 campaign)
California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO (2026 campaign)
California Teachers Association (2026 campaign)
California Nurses Association (2026 campaign)
San Francisco Chronicle Editorial Board (2026 campaign)
California Environmental Voters and Sierra Club Angeles Chapter (2026 campaign)
Equality California (2026 campaign)
YIMBY Action (2026 campaign)

cands.gaps: We found no documented position or action by Bonta on data centers, homestead property tax relief, limits on investor or foreign land buyers, school choice or teacher pay, police pay and pensions, or H-1B visas. We found no pledge to refuse donations from foreign-linked groups, PACs or developers. He did not complete Ballotpedia's Candidate Connection survey. The pages did not confirm his current State Bar standing. The pages gave no details on specific Attorney General lawsuits against the Trump administration beyond their number.

cands.name: Shirley N. Weber
cands.bio: California Secretary of State since January 2021, appointed by Gov. Newsom after Alex Padilla became a U.S. Senator. Previously represented Assembly District 79 (2012–2021). Former professor at San Diego State University, with other teaching posts at Cal State LA and Los Angeles City College. Holds three UCLA degrees, including a Ph.D.

endorsements.text: Ballotpedia lists 2026 endorsements from the Democratic Party of California, the California Federation of Labor Unions (AFL-CIO), the California Teachers Association, the California Nurses Association, SEIU Local 521, Equality California, California Environmental Voters, the Sierra Club Angeles Chapter and the San Francisco Chronicle Editorial Board.

cands.gaps: We found no record of Weber taking a position on data centers, homestead property taxes, foreign or investor land buying, growth and land conservation, immigration enforcement or H-1B, policing, gun laws or school choice. Her only documented stance on these topics is her support for the 2022 abortion-rights amendment. The pages we had show no controversies or foreign ties. Her birthplace, upbringing and move to California come from her own campaign website, and we found no independent source for them. We also could not confirm the year her family moved to California. She did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey, and her 2026 campaign site lists priorities but no specific policy positions on these topics.

local.label: Roots 90: Her campaign site says she was born in Hope, Arkansas, moved to Los Angeles at age three, and grew up in South LA; she also attended UCLA and later lived and worked in San Diego for decades.

races.title: Treasurer
races.note: The top two finishers from the Nov 3, 2026 count. Everyone else in this race is coming.

cands.name: Eleni Kounalakis
cands.bio: California's 50th Lieutenant Governor since 2019 and the first woman elected to that office. Former president of AKT Development, a Sacramento real estate firm. U.S. Ambassador to Hungary under President Obama. Elected State Treasurer on Nov. 3, 2026; takes office Jan. 4, 2027.

endorsements.text: Her campaign website lists Governor Gavin Newsom and the California Labor Federation as endorsers in the Treasurer race.

cands.gaps: We found no documented actions or stated positions from her on data centers, homestead property taxes, foreign or investor land buying, growth limits, immigration enforcement or H-1B, policing, gun laws, abortion, or school choice. No public statements on data centers or development were found. Ballotpedia reports no endorsements for the Treasurer race, so the only ones found come from her own campaign site. Her birthplace city and where she grew up were not found in any neutral source; the only indication of birth in California is her campaign site. Sources conflict slightly on when she left AKT Development and when she became ambassador. She did not complete Ballotpedia's 2026 candidate survey, so her platform comes only from her campaign site, which has little on policy.

local.label: Roots 55: Her campaign site calls her a native Californian, and the record shows her working in Sacramento real estate for nearly two decades and holding San Francisco appointments and statewide office since 2019, but no source states where she grew up.

score.why: Raised $0, under $50,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.

qual.background: Lieutenant Governor of California since 2019, including chairing the State Lands Commission and holding a seat on the UC Regents. Previously president of AKT Development, a Sacramento real estate and land development company, and U.S. Ambassador to Hungary (2010–2013). Holds a UC Berkeley MBA.
qual.why: She has held statewide executive office for seven years and has senior management experience running a large development company, which fits the high band for a statewide office.
qual.label: She has held statewide executive office for seven years and has senior management experience running a large development company, which fits the high band for a statewide office.

cands.bio: Republican candidate for California Treasurer in 2026. Describes herself as a retired businesswoman. She advanced from the June 2, 2026 primary to the general election, where she lost to Eleni Kounalakis (D). No prior elected office is documented.

endorsements.text: Ballotpedia lists endorsements from the Republican Party of California, the California Rifle & Pistol Association and Reform California, along with several voter-guide groups.

In her Ballotpedia survey, Hawks lists endorsements from the California Republican Assembly, the American Independent Party, Carl DeMaio and several county Republican parties (Santa Barbara, Madera, San Mateo, Silicon Valley, Santa Cruz, Napa). These are self-reported.

Her only stated positions are general ones on public finance: more transparency in the Treasurer's office, ending what she calls wasteful investments, and protecting worker retirement security. races.title: Controller

cands.name: Malia M. Cohen
cands.bio: California State Controller since January 2023. Previously served on the California State Board of Equalization (2019–2023) and the San Francisco Board of Supervisors (2011–2019). Born in San Francisco; earned degrees from Fisk University and Carnegie Mellon. Worked at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.

endorsements.text: Her 2026 endorsements, as listed by Ballotpedia, include former Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democratic Party of California, the California Federation of Labor Unions (AFL-CIO), the California Teachers Association, the California Nurses Association, SEIU Local 521, the San Francisco Chronicle Editorial Board, California Environmental Voters, Equality California and the Sierra Club Angeles Chapter.

cands.gaps: The pages we could read show no documented position or action by Cohen on data centers, development or growth limits, homestead property taxes, foreign or investor land buying, immigration or H-1B, guns, policing, school choice or teacher pay. They show no pledge about refusing particular kinds of donations. The only statements we could match to a platform topic concern reproductive health. Her campaign site names her issues but the detail pages did not load, so we could not read what she says under each. She did not complete Ballotpedia's 2026 candidate survey, and her 2022 survey is the most recent detailed statement we found. We found no documented controversies, foreign ties or lobbying in the sources we could read. We also could not confirm from the pages read when she moved to or lived outside California for school, though she says she was raised in San Francisco.

local.label: Roots 100: Ballotpedia and her campaign site both say she was born in San Francisco, and her campaign site and a 2022 candidate survey say she was raised there and attended its public schools.

score.why: Raised $0, under $50,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.

He said, "I didn't ask for this and don't welcome it."

CalMatters examined the 2024 state legislative journals to count absences. Those journals also record excused absences, which are often for illness or family matters. Allen's own total is in a chart that couldn't be read. No reason for his absences was found.

cands.name: Jane Kim
cands.bio: Attorney and Democrat. Served on the San Francisco Board of Education (2007–2011, including as president) and the Board of Supervisors for District 6 (2011–2019). Later worked as California political director for Bernie Sanders' 2020 campaign and as California director of the Working Families Party.

controversies.text: In June 2019 Kim and her 2014 re-election committee agreed to an $8,750 San Francisco Ethics Commission penalty for five violations. One was blurring office and campaign lines in newsletters that used office content. Staff found no evidence she acted willfully. In 2015 she had agreed to $5,700 and $2,500 penalties for campaign-finance violations.

In March 2022 San Francisco's Ethics Commission opened an investigation after a complaint that Kim, a former supervisor, lobbied against a 495-unit housing project without registering. She was paid as an organizer by nonprofit TODCO and sent supervisors materials from a TODCO affiliate. Kim says her opposition was on her own time. No finding is reported.

endorsements.text: U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, Working Families Party, California Teachers Association, California Nurses Association, National Union of Healthcare Workers, SEIU Local 521, Our Revolution and California Young Democrats (2026 Insurance Commissioner race, per Ballotpedia).

cands.gaps: We found no stated positions or actions by Jane Kim on data centers, homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign land buyers, immigration enforcement or H-1B visas, gun laws, abortion, or school vouchers and charters. platform.summary: This is the platform Ballot Buddy scores against, adapted to California. James Fishback ran on it in the 2026 Republican primary for Florida governor: an affordability and land-protection message on top of a conservative base. Details that only applied to Florida have been swapped for California. It's one yardstick, chosen by this guide, and not a neutral one.

planks.title: Ban data centers statewide
planks.promise: Ban AI and hyperscale data centers in every California county through statewide preemption of county approvals, to protect farmland, water and electric bills.
planks.tells_for: Votes or stated positions to ban, put a moratorium on, or preempt data-center approvals; opposing data-center rezonings on farmland; refusing data-center-industry money.
planks.tells_against: Votes to approve or fast-track a data center, rezone farmland for one, or give it tax breaks; campaigning on attracting data centers or AI infrastructure.

planks.title: Eliminate homestead property taxes
planks.promise: Eliminate property taxes on California residents' primary homes (not second homes, short-term rentals or mega-estates), paid for by rolling local government spending back.
planks.tells_for: Votes for homestead exemption increases, assessment caps or abolition; pledges to cut or end homestead taxes; pledges to cut local spending or tax rates.
planks.tells_against: Votes or statements for raising property taxes; opposing homestead tax relief; defending local government revenue growth.

planks.title: California homes and land for Californians
planks.promise: Ban private equity and Wall Street firms from buying single-family homes, tax out-of-state vacation-home buyers, and keep foreign adversaries from owning California land.
planks.tells_for: Supporting limits on institutional or foreign buyers of homes and land; proposing taxes or caps on out-of-state or investor purchases.
planks.tells_against: Opposing limits on corporate or foreign land buying; courting institutional or foreign real-estate capital.

planks.title: Slow growth, protect land and water
planks.promise: Develop slower and smarter, stop overdevelopment, and conserve California's state parks, waterways and natural lands.
planks.tells_for: Votes or statements to hold or tighten growth limits, require approvals for large developments, deny rezonings of farmland or open space, fund conservation; refusing developer money.
planks.tells_against: Votes to expand development boundaries, waive development oversight, preempt local growth limits, approve large developer land deals over resident objections; heavy developer funding.

planks.title: California workers first: end H-1B
planks.promise: End H-1B abuse with fines that wipe out any savings from replacing a California worker, keep H-1B workers off state contracts, raise foreign-student tuition, and back strong immigration enforcement and deportations.
planks.tells_for: Votes or statements for state cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, E-Verify, detention of criminal illegal immigrants, limiting H-1B or guest-worker displacement of Americans.
planks.tells_against: Votes or statements against immigration-enforcement bills; defending H-1B or guest-worker expansion or sanctuary-style policies.

planks.title: No foreign or big-donor money
planks.promise: Refuse contributions from foreign-affiliated groups (naming AIPAC) and run against donor capture.
planks.tells_for: Stated pledges to refuse foreign-linked, corporate-PAC, developer or out-of-state big-donor money; small-dollar funded campaigns.
planks.tells_against: Documented reliance on developer, foreign-linked or mega-donor or PAC money; stated openness to it.

planks.title: Back police, restore order
planks.promise: Raise pay and improve pensions for law enforcement and corrections officers, charge teen takeovers as felonies, surge state resources on homelessness, and remove prosecutors who refuse to prosecute.
planks.tells_for: Votes or positions raising penalties for rioting or disorder, funding or improving pay and pensions for officers, supporting police, tough-on-crime prosecution.
planks.tells_against: Votes cutting officer pensions or benefits; opposing penalties for public disorder; defund-style positions.

planks.title: Defend the Second Amendment
planks.promise: Eliminate Red Flag laws, end restrictions on suppressors, bump stocks and forced-reset triggers, and oppose raising gun purchase ages; also pull Flock cameras and stop Palantir contracts.
planks.tells_for: Votes for permitless carry and stand-your-ground, against red-flag laws and new purchase-age limits; pledges to oppose new gun restrictions.
planks.tells_against: Votes for red-flag laws, purchase-age or waiting-period laws, assault-weapon or magazine limits.

planks.title: Pro-life, no exceptions
planks.promise: Life begins at conception; shut down California's abortion clinics and replace them with crisis pregnancy centers, plus paid maternity leave.
planks.tells_for: Votes or statements for abortion bans, waiting periods or other abortion restrictions; support for pregnancy centers.
planks.tells_against: Votes or statements against abortion restrictions; support for abortion-access measures.

planks.title: School choice and teacher pay
planks.promise: Universal school choice funded toward parity with public schools, a state homeschool commissioner, and a 25% raise for teachers.
planks.tells_for: Votes or statements for vouchers, charters or universal choice and for raising teacher pay.
planks.tells_against: Votes or statements against voucher or charter expansion or school-choice funding.
